title: William Lee to James Monroe, Paris, 1, 2 and 6 February 1813 (NARA T164 roll 3): Lee's own numerical cipher, keyword WINCHESTER over a 25-letter alphabet; 1 Feb read, 2 and 6 Feb read in part, including 603 numerals of 6 Feb that carry no decipherment on this copy

steps.what: Andrew Beling contribution: the 2 Feb letter's source note in The Papers of James Monroe led to NARA T164 roll 3; frames 0095-0115 fetched; Lee's statement that he used his own cipher with the Secretary of State found in a certified copy (T1 roll 4 frames 0347-0348). The cipher was not yet analysed.

Andrew Beling contribution: the keyword WINCHESTER read from the clerk's pencilled key letters on 6 Feb (frames 0108-0109); the 25-letter alphabet and the rule (numeral - 1 + key letter, restart at each stretch) reproduce two pencilled words, DISTRESSING and MISFORTUNE, 21 of 21 letters; then 99 letters exact on selected passages of 1 and 6 Feb. Earliest record of the keyword in the project files; how it was first noticed is not recorded.
Andrew Beling contribution: 2 Feb transcribed in full, 41 stretches, 1,098 numerals; Y numeral 37 corrected to 4 on an enlarged crop.

Andrew Beling contribution: hand-chosen changes of key position inside 2 Feb stretches D, L, U, Y recover passages the clerk did not read (indemnities qualification; 'game now is to spin out the negotiations'; 'injudicious letter'; 'correspondence with the Dukes of Bassano and Dalberg', 45 of 45 letters); V gives 'his to Latrobe' with one wrong letter.

Andrew Beling contribution: one rule for every stretch replaces the hand-picking: the offset path maximising a letter 4-gram score minus 9.0 nats per change (penalty fixed before the first run), with 200 shuffled-numeral controls per stretch. 2 Feb: 33 of 38 stretches of 10 or more numerals beat all controls.

Andrew Beling contribution: 1 Feb (8 stretches, 110 numerals) and 6 Feb (74 stretches, 1,456 numerals) transcribed from full-resolution strips, decoded, and only then compared with the clerk's pencil; four numerals of 6 Feb and two of 1 Feb changed at 2x zoom, each marked.

Andrew Beling contribution: the same decoder and controls on 1 and 6 Feb: 71 of 82 stretches beat all 200 controls; the rest are short or the weak places listed in the gaps. Re-run on 10 Nov for this folder: every saved path and z reproduced.

Andrew Beling contribution: a second agent, without our files, re-read the never-deciphered part of 6 Feb (F6-43 to F6-74) from the frames: 588 of 589 numerals identical (F6-65 numeral 9: 1 or 17); one line of 14 numerals (F6-51) skipped by it.

Andrew Beling contribution: the three letters written out as sentences with Lee's clear text (checked on the frames), every repaired letter bracketed, the clerk's gaps and the slip-dependent passages marked. 1 Feb read; 2 and 6 Feb read in part under the strict bar (supplied letters counted as holes).

Andrew Beling contribution: 2 Feb J read as 'indemnities through' (key run on from I; a figure written 17 taken as 1 7; last figure re-read at zoom as 4), a proposal; N's '9231' divided 9 23 1, which gives 'now' with one key step instead of three; L's first word settled as 'their' (R left out with its key letter used); Z and AN numerals re-read on frame 0107; 6 Feb F6-01 'I established' (T used twice, 1.2 as 12) and F6-02 'a cipher, a copy' (11 as 1 1), proposals. errors.py gives for each stretch the cheapest set of Lee's mistakes that turns the reading into his figures; single wrong figures cluster under the key letter W (27 of 310 figures, 8.7%).

Andrew Beling read the three readings against the images (reading_review, grade A on each) and compared 1 Feb F1-H figures 21 and 23 on frame 0101 with Lee's other 10s and 16s: both 10, as transcribed (human_check).

Andrew Beling contribution: Weber 1979, Masked Dispatches, Cryptiana (293 pages), this repository's issues and pull requests, Papers of James Monroe vol. 6, web searches, and M. L. Mann, A Yankee Jeffersonian (1958), searched in full at HathiTrust (uc1.b4437374): no earlier identification of the cipher or keyword, no printing of the 1 or 6 Feb letters found; Mann does not mention the cipher.

Integration check by the project on merging PR #397: a decoder written separately from decode.py gives English for the 32 stretches F6-43 to F6-74 (603 numerals; 27 with the key restarted at W, 5 with a changed or carried-on key position); the three readings read as sentences; frames 0108-0110 fetched from the NARA catalogue and F6-15, F6-21, F6-22, F6-25, F6-30, F6-51 numerals 20-33, F6-65 to F6-69, part of F6-70 and F6-73, and F6-74 compared with the transcription at full resolution: all agree, so the single wrong letters there are on the page. The clerk's pencil is seen to stop at F6-42. The claim 'never deciphered at the time' narrowed: the letter is a Second Copy and no other copy was looked for.

outcome.method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext
outcome.method_basis: The keyword is the 1813 clerk's: he pencilled w i n c h e s t e r above the numerals of the 6 Feb letter, with his plaintext below (frames 0108-0109, a partial interlinear decipherment in the same file). The alphabet, the numeral rule, the restart and Lee's slips were worked out here against those pencilled words and then applied to all 123 stretches of the three letters, with shuffled-numeral controls.

parts.method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext

outcome.fraction_read_source: Cipher words of the three readings (528): 425 with no supplied, dropped, guessed or unread letter. Every word in which a letter Lee mis-enciphered is supplied counts as a hole (README read bar).

validation.notes: Contributor's test, not docs/_validate.py: per stretch, the decoder's score against 200 decodes of the same numerals shuffled (z and beats-all in each decryption file). 104 of 123 stretches beat all 200 (1 Feb 6/8, 2 Feb 33/41, 6 Feb 65/74); the failures are short stretches (5-15 numerals) and the weak places in gaps. Where the clerk read a passage, our decode agrees with his words except for the differences marked in the readings.

texts.label: Lee to Monroe, Paris, 1 Feb 1813 (private), T164 roll 3 frames 0099-0102, docket 0103
texts.summary: Lee attacks Warden's assumption of charge of the legation after Barlow's death: in cipher, the intrigues of the Irish Brigade and Marshal Sérurier on Warden's behalf, his use of Barlow's letter to Latrobe, toasts to the success of Clinton and Emmet, and his claim that the United Irishmen form a party so strong in the United States that the President dares not offend them.

reading_review.note: Read as sentences against frames 0099-0103; agrees with all readings. Checked F1-H figures 21 and 23 against Lee's other 10s and 16s: both 10.

texts.label: Lee to Monroe, Paris, 2 Feb 1813 ('Copy of Dispatch C'), T164 roll 3 frames 0106-0107
texts.summary: Barlow's treaty is to go before Napoleon, who would sanction it except for the indemnities the United States demands; France will spin out the negotiations and offer commercial advantages instead; Lee cites Barlow's correspondence with the Dukes of Bassano and Dalberg and cannot send a copy of the treaty.

reading_review.note: Read as sentences against frames 0104-0107; agrees with all readings, including the proposals marked §.

texts.label: Lee to the Secretary of State, Paris, 6 Feb 1813 ('Second Copy'), T164 roll 3 frames 0108-0110
texts.summary: France after the Russian disaster: the Grand Army destroyed, discontent, conscription and forced donations as the last effort of the nation, Austria's armed neutrality and possible mediation, Prussia's king fleeing the Russians, terms of peace offered to England if she abandons Russia, and Napoleon's hopes resting on the coming campaign. The last 32 stretches carry no decipherment on this copy, and none was found.

reading_review.note: Read as sentences against frames 0108-0110; agrees with all readings, including the proposals marked §.

outcome.notes: Contributed by Andrew Beling with AI agents. The 2 Feb letter is printed (Papers of James Monroe vol. 6) from the clerk's decipherment; 1 and 6 Feb were not found in print. Andrew Beling read the three readings as sentences against the images on 11 Nov 2026 (reading_review). read_share is the repo measure on the whole reading (clear text included); NOTES.md section 6 gives the cipher-only figures. Integration check, 11 Nov 2026 (NOTES.md): decryption of the 603 numerals re-derived with a separate decoder; about 300 numerals compared on frames 0108-0110; 'never deciphered at the time' narrowed to 'no decipherment on this copy, none found' because the letter is a Second Copy and no other copy was looked for.

human_check.note: Compared on the image, without AI help, with Lee's other 10s and 16s: both are 10, as transcribed (as 16 the word would be UFMEND, as 10 it is 'offend').

prior.where: The 1813 State Department clerk deciphered most of 2 Feb on separate sheets (frames 0104-0105; printed in The Papers of James Monroe vol. 6, MONR-01-06-02-0283) and pencilled a partial decipherment between the lines of pages 1-3 of 6 Feb; nothing for 1 Feb. No modern identification of the cipher or the keyword found: Weber 1979, Masked Dispatches, Cryptiana (293 pages), this repository, web searches (10-11 Nov 2026), and M. L. Mann, A Yankee Jeffersonian (1958), searched in full on 11 Nov 2026 (it does not print the February 1813 letters).

human: Andrew Beling set the tasks and the rules (numerals transcribed and decoded before the clerk's text was read; no silent repairs; nothing posted). AI agents located the frames, transcribed, decoded, compared and wrote; a further agent made the blind second reading of 6 Feb pp. 3-5. Andrew Beling read the three readings against the images (reading_review) and checked 1 Feb F1-H figures 21 and 23 on frame 0101 himself (human_check). No professional palaeographer has checked the numerals.
